name: Cirsium

project_scope.selection_mode: Genus Diagnostic Review — five learner taxa currently canonical

shared_traits: Spiny Asteraceae with discoid heads; the apparent flower is a head of many tubular florets.
Heads are enclosed by an involucre of overlapping phyllaries; phyllary shape, armature, orientation, and surface are high-value identification characters.
Cypselae bear a plumose pappus; mature fruit/pappus is useful for confirming Cirsium rather than relying on flower color.
genus_recognition.warning: Purple/pink flower color, overall plant height, generic 'woolliness', and disturbed-site habitat overlap strongly among learner taxa and should not be used alone.

look_here_first_sequence: 1. STEM: check whether leaf bases run down the stem as obvious spiny wings, and how long/continuous those wings are. NOTE: both Texas and bull thistles can have descending stem wings; use upper blade spines and head anatomy too.
2. HEAD BASE: inspect the involucre and any leaflike/spiny bracts immediately subtending the head; note phyllary spine length, orientation, and any glutinous ridge.
3. LEAF SURFACES: compare upper versus lower surfaces for green/glabrate, gray/white tomentose, or true short bristlelike spines.
4. LEAF SHAPE: record whether leaves are unlobed, shallowly pinnatifid, or deeply divided and whether the base clasps or is decurrent.
5. FRUIT/PAPPUS: use mature cypsela and plumose pappus when vegetative/head characters remain ambiguous.

diagnostic_matrix.look_here_first: Upper leaf surface plus stem wings.
strongest_separators: Only North American Cirsium in the FNA treatment with short appressed bristlelike spines arising from the adaxial leaf face.
Mid/distal leaves become decurrent as conspicuous spiny stem wings.
Large involucres about 3–4 cm long with radiating phyllary spines.

diagnostic_matrix.look_here_first: Armored collar directly below each large head.
strongest_separators: Each head is closely subtended by an involucre-like ring of spiny-margined bracts about as long as the involucre.
Main leaf spines are stout and may reach roughly 5–30 mm across the species complex.
Large involucres and heavily armed distal foliage create the characteristic armored-head architecture.

diagnostic_matrix.look_here_first: Decurrent wings plus long phyllary spines and woolly foliage.
strongest_separators: FNA keys the large-headed form with evidently decurrent mid/distal leaves forming spiny wings to about 5 cm.
Principal phyllary spines are commonly about 5–12 mm in the keyed large-headed form.
Tomentose foliage plus the combination of decurrent wings and strongly armed involucre is more useful than spine color alone.

diagnostic_matrix.look_here_first: Small involucre plus broad sessile/clasping upper leaves.
strongest_separators: FNA keys involucres around 1.2–2 cm in the Great Plains/eastern group.
Mid/distal cauline leaves are ovate and broadly sessile, sometimes auriculate-clasping or fully decurrent into spiny stem wings on robust specimens.
Use the relatively small head/involucre architecture together with leaf-base shape; do not identify from flower color.
unreliable_alone: absence or presence of descending spiny stem wings

diagnostic_matrix.look_here_first: Wavy/tomentose leaves, then confirm the involucre and fruit.
strongest_separators: FNA treats cauline leaves as ovate to lanceolate and subentire to coarsely toothed or shallowly lobed rather than relying on deeply cut leaves.
Cypselae are comparatively large, about 6–7 mm, with body and apical collar concolorous in the FNA key.
Confirm with the full leaf-surface and involucre character set because 'wavy gray leaf' appearance overlaps other western thistles.

comparison_notes: C. vulgare is the easiest high-confidence split when the adaxial leaf-face bristlelike spines are visible; this character is much stronger than general stem winging.
C. horridulum should be taught by the spiny bract collar around each head, not simply as 'the really spiny one.'
C. ochrocentrum and C. undulatum can both look gray/woolly; woolliness alone is therefore explicitly non-diagnostic.

C. texanum upper leaves can be auriculate-clasping AND on robust individuals can produce conspicuous spiny decurrent stem wings, as documented by UT Austin. Wing presence or length alone cannot cleanly separate it from introduced C. vulgare; the latter's UPPER-BLADE bristle-spines are stronger.

quick_key.if: Short stiff bristle-spines arising directly ON upper leaf BLADE (not just lobe edges); often with long decurrent spiny stem wings, which ALSO occur in robust native C. texanum
quick_key.then: Cirsium vulgare — introduced; leaf-FACE bristles best discriminator

quick_key.if: Large green involucre about 40–45 mm (UT Williamson var. horridulum); head hidden or ringed by extremely spiny reduced upper leaves
quick_key.then: Cirsium horridulum — extra head armor, not just a spiny stem

quick_key.if: Small green involucre about 15–20 mm tall (UT Williamson flora); broad sessile, sometimes auriculate-clasping upper leaves; some plants DO have spiny decurrent stem wings; no huge extra under-head collar
quick_key.then: Cirsium texanum — native Texas thistle; verify upper blade and head base

quick_key.if: Gray woolly plant, strongly spined phyllaries, often long spiny stem wings
Gray woolly plant, broader leaves often shallowly lobed, larger heads, fruit 6–7 mm
Only a rosette or critical character unclear

head_to_head.first: MEASURE THE GREEN INVOLUCRE: TEXANUM ~15–20 mm tall involucre versus HORRIDULUM var. horridulum ~40–45 mm tall in UT Williamson measured botanical descriptions. Measure the GREEN INVOLUCRAL BODY from its basal attachment to upper rim, excluding florets and projecting bract spines. Horridulum's separate, spinescent upper leaves/under-head collar obscure its large involucre; texanum has a smaller head and often clasping leaf bases, but CAN make winged stems.
head_to_head.photo: Licensed two-species SIDE/head source photos available but neither carries an original scale ruler; existing head photos may teach which part to measure, NOT visual proof of the numerical measurements. Matched ruler photos remain final polish.

head_to_head.first: Bull thistle uniquely has short appressed bristlelike spines growing on UPPER LEAF BLADE, and may have long spiny stem wings; Texas thistle on robust plants CAN ALSO have decurrent spiny wings (UT Austin). Do not teach wings alone as native/non-native test.
head_to_head.photo: Upper blade surface 10× plus wing extending down a full stem internode.

head_to_head.first: Both woolly. Ochrocentrum: strong phyllary spines often 5–12 mm and some strongly decurrent spiny leaves; undulatum: broader often shallowly lobed leaves and mature 6–7 mm fruits.
head_to_head.photo: Paired phyllary tips with scale; stem wing, full leaves, and undulatum mature cypsela.

head_to_head.pair: C. texanum vs C. carolinianum (comparison only)
head_to_head.first: Texanum: broad sessile/auriculate upper leaves; carolinianum: narrow cuneate/tapered upper leaf bases. Both can have involucres ~12–20 mm.

visual_comparison.memory_rule: HORRIDULUM = extra spiny collar; VULGARE = short spines on UPPER LEAF FACE; TEXANUM = smaller head, broad sessile upper leaves; OCHROCENTRUM = wool and long phyllary spines; UNDULATUM = broad leaves and large ripe fruit.

autumn_rosette_lesson.first: Seedheads/rosettes can be more visible than flowers this season. Look for rosette from above + leaf upper/lower face and stem remnants.
steps: Photograph rosette from straight overhead and side, with ruler and a leaf tip.
Photograph upper and lower leaf surfaces under lens: bull thistle bristlelike spines IN blade are high-value; underside wool is not species-exclusive.
If mature stem survives, document downward stem wings and the base of old head for collar.
Do not assign native/non-native from a photo of purple head or rosette wool alone.

key: C. vulgare: bristlelike short spines on upper LEAF FACE are the decisive diagnostic. Winged stems alone occur in other thistles.
C. horridulum: look for separate spiny BRACT COLLAR immediately below EACH head, as opposed to phyllaries constituting the head itself.
C. texanum: smaller 12–20 mm green involucre; broad sessile or ear-clasping cauline leaf bases, often sticky/milky glutinous ridge on outside of outer/middle phyllaries.
remaining: Matched true side-profile photograph of C. texanum with ruler showing 12–20 mm involucre, excluding floral tuft.
